1970 Ford Mustang Mach 1 R-Code 428 Cobra Jet Begs for Restoration After Years in Hiding
28 photos
Photo: eBay seller hbmustangs
I don’t know about you, but every time I see a 1970 Mustang, I think about Ford’s marketing campaign that insisted on how buying a Mustang could have changed your life. And this Mach 1 did just that, making me think of those times when Ford thought it was cool to tell guys that buying a new car would have helped them for… you know.
“Marc Muccino’s coaching career was a big ‘zero’ until he bought his Mustang SportsRoof. Now it’s a whole new ball game,” Ford said in one of these Mustang booklets, showing a man surrounded by attractive women.
I do admit that the 1970 Mustang was a gorgeous car, despite not sporting all that many changes from the previous. This made sense, considering the 1969 model year witnessed the introduction of a major makeover, but the 1970 model year somehow brought this release to maturity.
This Mach 1 is here because it needs a second chance to re-become this awesome car that once turned heads everywhere. We don’t know much about its past, but it certainly looks like it’s been sitting for more than just a couple of years in a place away from humanity.
It needs a complete restoration, and the thing that caught my attention was the R-coded setup. This car was once powered by the 428 Cobra Jet, the second-best engine you could get in 1970.
Photo: eBay seller hbmustangs Ford offered not one, not two, but nine different engine choices in 1970. Two sixes - a 200 with 120 horsepower and a 250 with 155 horsepower - were specifically aimed at those buyers who cared more about the looks than the power under the hood.
The 302 rated at 220 horsepower marked the foray into the V8 business, while the Boss version of the same engine provided more adrenaline behind the wheel thanks to an increase to 290 horsepower.
The 351 was available in two versions. The two-barrel configuration went as high as 250 horsepower, while the four-barrel sibling produced 300 horsepower.
Then, the big guys showed up.
The 428 Cobra produced 335 horsepower, but Ford also offered the same output on the 428 Cobra Jet. Both engines could only be ordered with a SelectShift or a 4-speed manual close-ratio transmission.
The top choice was the 429 Boss with 375 horsepower.
Photo: eBay seller hbmustangs This Mach 1 was once powered by the Cobra Jet, but that’s no longer the case today. The only thing you’ll find in the engine bay is a lot of fresh air. The seller doesn’t share additional details, but I wouldn’t be surprised to learn that the engine and the transmission were both removed to be donated to another Mach 1 that was being restored.
The car has clearly been sitting for a while, and the owner says it from the very beginning. It “needs a lot of rust repairs,” and there’s no doubt this is true.
This isn’t an easy project, especially if you want to restore it to factory specifications. There’s another reason why you’ll want to stick with the original settings, as the car was wearing the rare Pastel Blue paired with a blue interior.
And speaking about the interior, it’s mostly complete, though it goes without saying that using everything for restoration wouldn’t be possible. My advice is to call the seller and maybe ask for more details, and if you don’t live very far, you should also go there in person and see the car with your own eyes.
Photo: eBay seller hbmustangs Otherwise, it’s hard to be disappointed if you know what to expect. This Mustang is a massive project that would be worth the effort once done right.
This wasn’t an affordable car and still isn’t. The hardtop was the most affordable Mustang version in 1970, carrying a starting price of $2,721, while the fastback was next with a base price of $2,771. The Grand was next with $2,926 for the base configuration, while the top choices, the Mach 1 and the convertible, surpassed the $3K threshold.
The convertible started at $3,025, while the Mach 1 was available from $3,271. The more options you added, the higher the price went, so for example, if you wanted the top 429 with 375 horsepower, you had to pay no more, no less than $1,208 more on your Mustang.
Photo: eBay seller hbmustangs This Mustang can be yours for $12,850, but the seller has also enabled the Make Offer option on eBay, so you can try your luck and see if they accept your offer if you have another deal in mind. The car is parked in Aragon, Georgia, and you should also consider shipping costs, given that the engine is no longer there, so the car does not run.
The listing will expire in 24 days, so you have all the time in the world to convince your wife that you need this car and the seller to accept your offer.
